summary: APOLO is an offline-first health companion that helps astronauts assess their own health during long missions, without a doctor or a live link to Earth. A friendly astronaut-dog assistant sits at the center of the screen and talks with each crew member by voice or text. Health indicators float around it as circles, color-coded green (stable), yellow (attention) or red (critical), always with an icon and a word, never color alone. Only the indicators that need attention appear at first; the rest show up when the astronaut asks. APOLO combines urine biomarkers (hydration, kidney-stone risk, bone loss, radiation damage, infection, stress and sleep, metabolism) with vital signs, radiation dosimetry from NASA standards and space-weather alerts from NASA DONKI, and turns them into simple personalized actions like "drink 500 ml in the next two hours". This matters because on missions to the Moon and Mars, communication delays make real-time help from flight surgeons impossible, so crews must detect problems early and act on their own.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

APOLO lets each crew member check their health in seconds and know exactly what to do. An animated astronaut dog greets the astronaut and summarizes their status. Floating circles around it show the health indicators that need attention, sorted by urgency and colored green (stable), yellow (attention) or red (critical), always with an icon and a word. Tapping a circle opens a card with the key value, each biomarker's personal range, a trend of recent samples, a checklist of actions and a short explanation of why it matters in space. The astronaut can talk to APOLO by voice or text ("How am I?", "How are my kidneys?", "I drank 500 ml", "I did 30 minutes of exercise"). Every answer and every clinical test the assistant launches (motion-sickness questionnaire, reaction-time test, vision tests, voice diary) also appears as a circle that can be opened, read aloud or hidden. A countdown reminds the crew when the next urine sample is due, and a clinical modules area gives deeper views of vital signs, radiation dosimetry, microgravity countermeasures, sleep and mental health, and autonomous triage.

HOW IT WORKS

A deterministic engine computes 8 health circles from 23 urine biomarkers (hydration, kidney-stone risk, bone resorption, radiation oxidative damage, immunity, cardiovascular salt balance, stress and sleep hormones, metabolism), compared with each astronaut's personal baseline. Vital signs, radiation dose (NASA-STD-3001 limits) and space-weather alerts (NASA DONKI) feed the clinical modules. A clinical agent with skills and tools decides which circles and tests to show. When the Earth link is down, deterministic offline flows answer the same questions and log water, exercise and samples on the device. All crew data stays on the device.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Fast self-assessment with no medical training; early warning of problems that escalate on long missions (kidney stones, bone loss, radiation exposure, infection, sleep debt); less cognitive load because stable systems stay hidden until asked; hands-free use by voice. Our goal is a companion crews can trust on the way to the Moon and Mars, where communication delays prevent real-time help from flight surgeons.

TOOLS

Flutter and Dart (Android, web, desktop), Riverpod, Hive (offline storage), fl_chart, speech_to_text and flutter_tts; a Python FastAPI voice gateway with an LLM, faster-whisper (speech-to-text) and Kokoro/Piper (text-to-speech); HTML/CSS/JavaScript for the first web prototype; Figma for UI exploration; GitHub for collaboration.

CREATIVITY

Instead of a dense medical dashboard, APOLO is a friendly mascot that reacts to the astronaut's health (happy, worried, sweating when something is critical) and shows information only when it is needed, like a conversation. Health data, answers and tests all share one visual language: floating circles.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Offline-first operation for deep space; astronauts are not doctors, so every value comes with a plain-language explanation and a concrete action; accessibility in the cockpit (high-contrast mode, reduced motion, large touch targets, never color alone); responsive design from cabin tablets to laptops; and scientific grounding in NASA standards and data. Demo crew data is synthetic and thresholds should be validated by medical experts.
